newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan parliament demands member quit over indictment.
newsitem.headline: Japan parliament demands member quit over indictment.

text.p: Japan's parliament on Friday passed its first-ever resolution calling on one of its lawmakers to resign his seat after the legislator refused to quit following a fraud indictment.
But one member of parliament opposed what would otherwise have been a unanimous resolution in the 252-member Upper House seeking the resignation of lawmaker Tatsuo Tomobe.
Upper House lawmaker Michio Sato, a retired prosecutor, cast the only "No" vote in the non-binding resolution.

"He hasn't even been found guilty," Sato, an independent, said after the vote in the full Upper House. "Is it right for parliament to quash the grand prerequisite of presumed innocence in a criminal trial?"

Tomobe, his son and two other executives of his Orange Kyosai mutual aid fund have been charged with swindling 33 depositors of about 620 million yen ($5 million). Tomobe has refused to resign from his seat in parliament.
The resolution said the Upper House believes Tomobe is guilty.

"Legislator Tomobe bears great political and ethical liability for cheating customers of Orange Kyosai Kumiai which he has virtually run," the resolution said. It was the first-ever resolution passed by either chamber in Japan's parliament calling on one of its members to quit.

Sato accused the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) of hypocrisy in pushing the resolution because the party has not asked LDP Lower House member Takao Fujinami, who was convicted last month for his role in a 1989 bribery case, to quit.
"There is no such move in the Lower House over Mr. Fujinami, mainly because the LDP is trying to cover up that case," Sato said.

Fujinami, chief cabinet secretary under former Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone, was convicted of taking bribes from publishing house Recruit Co. He was given a suspended prison sentence, meaning he need not serve the term on condition of good public conduct.
